title: Welcome
note: Pick one and hold your answer. It is settled in the last room, not before.

cues.show: Welcome. In front of you, on the tatami, lies a single roll of cloth.
The hall around you is a reconstructed room in the Edo-period shoin style, not any one building.
cues.say: The hall around you is a reconstructed room in the Edo-period show-in style, not any one building.

cues.show: The word kimono is plain Japanese. Kiru, to wear. Mono, a thing. A thing to wear.
cues.say: The word kimono is plain Japanese. Kee-roo, to wear. Moh-noh, a thing. A thing to wear.

cues.show: So the question here may sound strange. Is a kimono a garment, or a set of rules?
Choose one now, and hold on to it. The rooms ahead will test your answer. Only the last one settles it.
Begin with the roll. Everything in the next room is made from it, and from nothing else.

claims.text: The word kimono comes from kiru mono: kiru, to wear; mono, a thing.
claims.quote: The word kimono derives from the Japanese 'kiru mono', with kiru meaning 'to wear' and mono being 'a thing'.

claims.text: One bolt of cloth makes one kimono.
claims.quote: １反（幅約 36～38cm・長さ約 12m）という単位で扱い，１反がキモノ１枚分に相当する
claims.scope: Tr.: "handled in units of one tan (width about 36-38 cm, length about 12 m); one tan equals one kimono". General statement for a woman's nagagi, the authors citing a tailoring textbook.
